title: Concurrency and Asynchronous Programming in Python
subtitle: Make Python do many things at once, correctly: threads, processes and asyncio, and the measurements that tell you which to use.
outcomes: Explain how processes, threads and the GIL decide what runs in parallel in CPython, including Python 3.13's optional free-threaded build
Write threaded code that stays correct under contention, with locks, queues and thread pools from concurrent.futures
Speed up CPU-bound Python with process pools, keeping the cost of copying data under control
Build asyncio programs with tasks, TaskGroup, timeouts, cancellation, async context managers and bounded concurrency
Call HTTP APIs concurrently with httpx, with timeouts, retries and tests that need no network
Find and prevent race conditions and deadlocks, and choose the right concurrency model for a workload
prerequisites: Confident Python: functions, classes, exceptions, context managers, modules and virtual environments, as in Python Programming with PyCharm. Introduction to FastAPI and Modern Web Services uses async def at an introductory level; this course explains what happens underneath. You need Python 3.11 or later (3.13 recommended), any editor, and httpx and pytest installed in a virtual environment (pip install httpx pytest).
description:
Most programs spend their time waiting, for the network, the disk or a database, and others are held back by a single busy CPU core. This course teaches the three ways Python deals with both, and when to use each: threads, processes and asyncio. It starts with how the operating system runs processes and threads and what CPython's global interpreter lock (GIL) does, including the optional free-threaded build that arrived in Python 3.13. Then it works through threading and locks, thread and process pools from concurrent.futures, and multiprocessing for CPU-bound work. The second half is asyncio: the event loop, tasks, gather and TaskGroup, timeouts and cancellation, async context managers, queues and semaphores, and concurrent HTTP calls with httpx.

Every module has a lab with starter code, and checks that look at results rather than timings, so they pass on any machine: fix an overselling box office with a lock, spread a CPU-bound search over every core, build an async job runner with time limits, and write a polite, retrying HTTP client tested against a fake server. The last module shows how race conditions and deadlocks happen in each model and how to prevent them, and how to choose a model from measurements. The capstone brings it all together: an aggregator that crawls a slow, unreliable local API with asyncio and scores the results in a process pool. Afterwards, Advanced FastAPI and Production Deployment puts these ideas to work in a web service.

modules.title: Processes, threads and the GIL
modules.summary: Why concurrency speeds some programs up and not others: I/O-bound and CPU-bound work, how processes and threads differ, and what CPython's global interpreter lock and the new free-threaded build mean for parallel Python.

lessons.title: Concurrency, parallelism and where the time goes
objectives: Distinguish concurrency from parallelism
Classify a workload as I/O-bound or CPU-bound by measuring it
Explain the costs that concurrency adds
key_points: Concurrency means a program has several tasks in progress at once and interleaves them; parallelism means tasks run at the same instant on different CPU cores. Concurrency is a way to structure a program; parallelism needs the hardware to run it.
An I/O-bound task spends most of its time waiting: for a network reply, a disk or a database. Overlapping those waits speeds it up even on a single core, which is what threads and asyncio do.

A CPU-bound task keeps a core busy computing, as hashing, parsing and numeric loops do. Only running parts of it on several cores at once, in separate processes or in native code that releases the GIL, makes it finish sooner.

time.perf_counter() measures elapsed (wall-clock) time and time.process_time() the CPU time the process has used. If CPU time is far below elapsed time, the program is mostly waiting, so it's I/O-bound.

Concurrency has costs: starting threads or processes, coordinating them, and new kinds of bug, such as race conditions, that are hard to reproduce. Measure first, and add concurrency only where waiting or computing is the bottleneck.

walkthrough.title: Measure elapsed time against CPU time

steps.do: Save this script as where_time_goes.py. It times one job that waits and one that computes, measuring both elapsed time and CPU time.
Run it.
steps.see: wait_for_io takes about 0.50s elapsed but close to 0.00s of CPU; crunch_numbers uses CPU for most of its elapsed time (a little less if other programs are busy).

steps.do: Add a third job that mixes the two, such as a loop of 20 steps that sleeps 0.02 seconds and then sums 100,000 squares on each step. Run the script again and decide from the two numbers whether it's mostly waiting or mostly computing.
For a real program, profile it to see which functions the time goes to. cProfile comes with Python; sort its table by cumulative time.
steps.see: A table of calls in which {built-in method time.sleep} and crunch_numbers account for almost all of the time.

lessons.title: Processes and threads
objectives: Explain how processes and threads differ in memory, isolation and cost
Start a thread and a process from Python and wait for them
key_points: A process is a running program with its own memory. The operating system keeps processes apart, so one can't corrupt another's data, and they share data only by explicit means: pipes, sockets, files or shared memory.

A thread is a sequence of instructions running inside a process. All the threads of a process share its memory and objects, which makes sharing data fast, but means changes to shared data need coordinating.
Starting a process costs more than starting a thread: a new Python process has to start an interpreter and import modules, and any data passed to it is copied, usually by pickling.

The operating system's scheduler decides when each thread runs and can switch between them at almost any moment (pre-emptive multitasking), so code that runs in threads must be correct whatever the interleaving.

threading.Thread(target=f, args=(x,)) and multiprocessing.Process(target=f, args=(x,)) share an interface: start() begins the work and join() waits for it to finish. os.getpid() tells you which process code is running in.

walkthrough.title: See that threads share memory and processes don't

steps.do: Save share_or_copy.py. The worker appends to a module-level list and reports whether it's running in the parent's process.
steps.code:
import multiprocessing
import os
import threading

shared = []


def worker(label, parent_pid):
    shared.append(label)
    print(f"{label}: same process as the parent? {os.getpid() == parent_pid}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    t = threading.Thread(target=worker, args=("thread", os.getpid()))
    t.start()
    t.join()
    print("after the thread: ", shared)

    p = multiprocessing.Process(target=worker, args=("process", os.getpid()))
    p.start()
    p.join()
    print("after the process:", shared)

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: The thread says True and its append is visible afterwards: ['thread']. The process says False, and its append happened only in its own copy of the list, which is still ['thread'] in the parent.

steps.do: Add a line to worker that prints threading.current_thread().name, and run it again.
steps.see: thread runs in Thread-1 (worker), but process runs in MainThread: a new process starts with a main thread of its own.

steps.do: Note what each start cost: time the two starts with time.perf_counter() around start() and join(). The process takes noticeably longer, because a new interpreter has to start.

lessons.title: The GIL and the free-threaded build
objectives: Explain what the GIL does and what it doesn't protect
Describe Python 3.13's free-threaded build and check which build you're running
key_points: CPython, the standard Python interpreter, has a global interpreter lock (GIL): only one thread at a time runs Python bytecode in a process. So pure-Python CPU-bound code doesn't run faster with more threads.

A thread releases the GIL while it waits for I/O (sockets, files, time.sleep), and many C extensions release it during long operations, such as hashlib on large data, zlib and NumPy. That's why threads still speed up I/O-bound work.
The GIL doesn't make your code thread-safe. A thread can be switched out between the read and the write of counter += 1, so shared data that changes still needs a lock.

Python 3.13 added an optional free-threaded build of CPython (PEP 703), installed separately and often run as python3.13t, in which the GIL is disabled and threads can run Python code on several cores at once. In 3.13 it is marked experimental.

sys._is_gil_enabled() (3.13 and later) says whether the GIL is on, and sysconfig.get_config_var('Py_GIL_DISABLED') is 1 on a free-threaded build. That build turns the GIL back on if it imports an extension module not marked as safe without it, unless run with PYTHON_GIL=0 or -X gil=0.

The free-threaded build trades some single-threaded speed for parallelism, and C extensions need builds made for it. Python 3.14 made it officially supported but still optional: the default build, with the GIL, is what most installations run.

walkthrough.title: Check your build, and watch the GIL at work

steps.do: Print the full version string. A free-threaded build mentions free-threading in it.
steps.see: Something like Python 3.13.x (main, ...) [GCC ...] on the default build.

steps.do: Save gil_check.py and run it with python gil_check.py.
steps.code:
import sys
import sysconfig

print("Python", sys.version.split()[0])
print("free-threaded build:", bool(sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED")))
print("GIL enabled now:", sys._is_gil_enabled())      # Python 3.13 and later
steps.see: On the default build: free-threaded build: False and GIL enabled now: True.

steps.do: Save gil_threads.py. It counts down from ten million in one thread, then splits the same work between four threads.
steps.code:
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor


def count_down(n):
    while n:
        n -= 1


N = 10_000_000
start = time.perf_counter()
count_down(N)
print(f"one thread, all the work:   {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")

start = time.perf_counter()
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
    list(pool.map(count_down, [N // 4] * 4))
print(f"four threads, a quarter each: {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: On the default build the two times are about the same: the four threads take turns holding the GIL, so there's no speed-up.

steps.do: If you have a free-threaded build (the python.org installers for Windows and macOS offer it as an option), run the same script with it.
steps.see: With the GIL disabled, the four-thread run can finish sooner on a machine with several cores, because the threads really do run in parallel.

lab.title: Profile I/O-bound and CPU-bound work three ways
lab.goal: Run the same I/O-bound job and CPU-bound job sequentially, in a thread pool and in a process pool, write the process-pool version yourself, and explain from your own measurements which model helps which kind of work.
setup: Python 3.11 or later in a virtual environment (3.13 or later reports the GIL's status)
The starter file three_ways.py in a folder of its own
A computer with at least two CPU cores, with nothing else heavy running while you measure

steps.do: Read three_ways.py. fake_download waits like a network call; count_primes keeps a core busy. run_sequential and run_threads are written for you.
Write run_processes: create a ProcessPoolExecutor with max_workers=workers in a with block, map fn over jobs, and return the results as a list, in the order of jobs.
Run the script. Every line must show the same answer for its kind of job, whichever method ran it.
steps.see: A line with the Python version and GIL enabled:, then six lines: io ... squares=140 and cpu ... primes=17984, each with its time.

steps.do: Run it twice more and put the times in a table, method by workload. Times vary from run to run, so look at the pattern rather than the exact numbers.
Call run_threads and run_processes with workers=8 instead of 4 (change the defaults) and run it again. Note which times change, and why.
Write two or three sentences under each of the headings I/O-bound: and CPU-bound:, saying which method was fastest and why, in terms of waiting, the GIL and the cost of starting processes.

checks.text: Every method gives the same results: squares=140 for the I/O-bound job and primes=17984 for the CPU-bound job.
run_processes uses a ProcessPoolExecutor and returns the results in input order.
The output reports the Python version and whether the GIL is enabled.
The explanation says which method was fastest for each workload and why: threads overlap the waits of I/O-bound work, and on the default build only processes run CPU-bound Python in parallel.

lab.submit: Paste your run_processes function, the output of one run of python three_ways.py, your table of times, and your sentences under I/O-bound: and CPU-bound:.
hints: pool.map returns an iterator over the results, in the same order as the inputs; wrap it in list() to collect them all.
If you see a RuntimeError about the bootstrapping phase (on Windows or macOS), the code that starts processes isn't protected by if __name__ == "__main__":.
Times depend on whatever else the computer is doing. Close other heavy programs and repeat each measurement; on the default build, threads give pure-Python CPU-bound work no real speed-up.

modules.title: Threads: locks, queues and thread pools
modules.summary: Use threads safely: hand work between them with thread-safe queues, protect shared state with locks and the other synchronisation primitives, and let concurrent.futures manage a pool of threads and their results.

lessons.title: Threads and thread-safe queues
objectives: Start, join and hand work between threads
Build a producer-consumer pipeline with queue.Queue
Explain what happens to exceptions and daemon threads
key_points: threading.Thread(target=fn, args=(...)) creates a thread; start() runs fn in it and join() waits for it to finish. A thread's return value is thrown away, so results come back through a queue or a shared structure protected by a lock.

queue.Queue is thread-safe: put() and get() do their own locking, get() blocks until an item is available, and Queue(maxsize=n) makes put() block while n items are waiting, which stops a fast producer running ahead (back-pressure).

In a producer-consumer pipeline, consumers loop on get() and call task_done() for every item; q.join() returns once every item put has been marked done, and a sentinel value such as None, one per consumer, tells each consumer to stop.

A daemon thread (Thread(..., daemon=True)) is stopped abruptly when the program exits, without running its finally blocks, so use daemon threads only for work that's safe to lose, and join the others for a clean shutdown.

An exception raised in a thread doesn't reach the code that started it: threading.excepthook prints it and the thread ends. Catch errors inside the thread, or use concurrent.futures, which hands them back to you.

steps.do: Save queue_pipeline.py: the main thread produces ten numbers and three consumer threads square them.
steps.code:
import queue
import threading

STOP = None                      # a sentinel: tells a consumer to finish


def consumer(q, results, lock):
    while True:
        item = q.get()
        try:
            if item is STOP:
                return
            with lock:
                results.append(item * item)
        finally:
            q.task_done()


q = queue.Queue(maxsize=5)       # put() blocks while 5 items are waiting
results, lock = [], threading.Lock()
workers = [threading.Thread(target=consumer, args=(q, results, lock)) for _ in range(3)]
for w in workers:
    w.start()
for item in range(10):           # the producer
    q.put(item)
for _ in workers:
    q.put(STOP)                  # one sentinel per consumer
q.join()                         # every item, sentinels included, is done
for w in workers:
    w.join()
print(f"processed {len(results)} items, total {sum(results)}")

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: processed 10 items, total 285

steps.do: Comment out the loop that puts the sentinels and run it again.
steps.see: Nothing is printed and the program hangs: the consumers wait for items that never come, and Python waits for them before it exits. Press Ctrl+C (twice if needed), then put the loop back.

steps.do: Make a consumer fail: add if item == 7: raise ValueError(item) just before with lock:, and run it.
steps.see: A traceback starting Exception in thread Thread-... (consumer) and ending ValueError: 7, and then a hang: the dead consumer never takes its sentinel, so q.join() waits for ever. Press Ctrl+C and remove the line.

lessons.title: Locks and other synchronisation primitives
objectives: Explain how a lost update happens
Protect shared state with Lock and RLock
Choose between Event, Semaphore, Barrier and Condition
key_points: counter += 1 is three steps: read the value, add one, write it back. If two threads both read before either writes, one update is lost. A bug whose outcome depends on how threads happen to interleave is a race condition.

threading.Lock protects a critical section: with lock: lets one thread in at a time and releases the lock even if the block raises. Keep critical sections short, and never wait for slow I/O while holding a lock.

A thread that tries to acquire a plain Lock it already holds waits for ever. threading.RLock, a re-entrant lock, can be acquired again by the thread that holds it, which helps when one locked method calls another.

Event lets threads wait for a signal (wait() until another thread calls set()); Semaphore(n) lets at most n threads into a section; Barrier(n) holds threads until n have arrived; Condition lets threads wait until shared state changes, re-checking it in a while loop.
The safest shared state is none at all: give each thread its own data and combine the results at the end, pass messages through a queue.Queue, or keep per-thread values in threading.local().

walkthrough.title: Make a race happen, then fix it with a lock

steps.do: Save lost_update.py. Four threads each add one to a shared counter 1,000 times; time.sleep(0) between the read and the write invites a thread switch at the worst moment.
steps.code:
import threading
import time

ROUNDS, THREADS = 1000, 4
counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()


def unsafe_increment():
    global counter
    for _ in range(ROUNDS):
        value = counter          # read
        time.sleep(0)            # invite a thread switch between the read and the write
        counter = value + 1      # write


def safe_increment():
    global counter
    for _ in range(ROUNDS):
        with lock:               # the read and the write happen as one step
            value = counter
            time.sleep(0)
            counter = value + 1


for fn in (unsafe_increment, safe_increment):
    counter = 0
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=fn) for _ in range(THREADS)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()
    print(f"{fn.__name__}: {counter} (expected {ROUNDS * THREADS})")

steps.do: Run it a few times.
steps.see: unsafe_increment ends far below 4000, with a different total on each run; safe_increment prints 4000 (expected 4000) every time.

steps.do: Delete the time.sleep(0) line from unsafe_increment and run it again.
steps.see: Probably 4000 every time now. The race is still there, only much rarer, which is exactly what makes races so hard to catch in testing.

steps.do: Put that line back. In safe_increment, nest a second with lock: inside the first (indent the three lines under it) and run the script.
steps.see: unsafe_increment prints as before, then the program hangs: a thread can't acquire a Lock it already holds. Press Ctrl+C (twice if needed).

steps.do: Change lock = threading.Lock() to lock = threading.RLock() and run it again.
steps.see: safe_increment: 4000 (expected 4000): a re-entrant lock can be taken again by its holder.

lessons.title: Thread pools with concurrent.futures
objectives: Run blocking calls concurrently with ThreadPoolExecutor
Collect results and errors with futures, map and as_completed
Size a thread pool for the resource it uses
key_points: concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=n) keeps a pool of threads and reuses them for many tasks. Used as a context manager, it waits for all the submitted work and shuts the pool down when the with block ends.
pool.submit(fn, *args) returns a Future straight away; future.result(timeout=None) waits for the value and re-raises any exception fn raised, so errors aren't lost as they are in a bare thread.

pool.map(fn, items) yields results in input order and raises a task's exception when you reach its result; as_completed(futures) yields futures as they finish, so the quickest results can be handled first.

Without max_workers, ThreadPoolExecutor uses min(32, number of CPUs + 4) threads, a default meant for I/O-bound work. Size the pool from what the resource can take, such as the number of connections a database allows.

future.cancel() only stops a task that hasn't started, and pool.shutdown(cancel_futures=True) (Python 3.9+) cancels everything still queued. A running thread can't be killed, so a long task should check a threading.Event to know when to stop.
ThreadPoolExecutor and ProcessPoolExecutor share the Executor interface (submit, map, shutdown and Future objects), so moving work from threads to processes is often a one-line change.

steps.do: Save pool_futures.py. Three lookups take different times, and one of them fails.
Run it.
steps.see: Results in the order they finish: fast: found, then broken: error: lookup failed, then slow: found.

steps.do: Replace the four lines from futures = to the end of the except block with a loop over pool.map, and run it again.
steps.code:
for result in pool.map(lookup, jobs, jobs.values()):
        print(result)
steps.see: slow: found and fast: found, in input order, then a ConnectionError: lookup failed traceback when the loop reaches the broken lookup's result.

steps.do: Undo that change, set max_workers=1 and run it again.
steps.see: slow: found, fast: found, broken: error: lookup failed: with one thread the lookups run one at a time, in the order they were submitted.

lab.title: Fix an overselling box office, then pool a slow service
lab.goal: Find and fix a check-then-act race with a lock, then make twelve blocking calls run concurrently with a ThreadPoolExecutor, keeping every result and every error.
setup: The starter files box_office.py and reports.py in one folder

steps.do: Run box_office.py a few times. Eight customer threads each try to buy 50 tickets for a show with 100 seats.
steps.see: Usually more than 100 sold and seats left below 0, followed by OVERSOLD, with different numbers on each run.

steps.do: Above buy(), write a comment that explains the bug: which two steps can another thread get between?

Run it several times.
steps.see: sold 100, refused 300, seats left 0 and no seat sold twice, on every run.

lab.submit: Paste your BoxOffice class with its comment, fetch_all_concurrently, the output of three runs of box_office.py and one of reports.py, and a sentence on how you'd choose max_workers for a real service.

files.content:
"""A box office that sells tickets from several threads at once. It oversells: fix it."""
import threading
import time


class BoxOffice:
    def __init__(self, seats):
        self.seats = seats
        self.sold = 0
        self.refused = 0
        # TODO: create a lock for the box office
        pass

    def buy(self):
        # TODO: hold the lock around the whole check-then-update, so no other
        #       thread can sell the same seat in between.
        if self.seats > 0:
            time.sleep(0)            # a thread switch here is what makes the race likely
            self.seats -= 1
            self.sold += 1
            return True
        self.refused += 1
        return False


def customer(office, attempts):
    for _ in range(attempts):
        office.buy()


def main():
    office = BoxOffice(seats=100)
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=customer, args=(office, 50)) for _ in range(8)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()
    print(f"sold {office.sold}, refused {office.refused}, seats left {office.seats}")
    print("OVERSOLD" if office.sold > 100 else "no seat sold twice")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: Create the lock once, in __init__, so every thread shares it; a lock created inside buy() would protect nothing.
A task's exception comes out of future.result(): wrap that call in try/except ValueError.
as_completed yields futures in the order they finish, so sort the reports by id before returning them.

modules.title: Processes for CPU-bound work
modules.summary: Use every core for CPU-bound Python with multiprocessing and ProcessPoolExecutor: start methods and the main-module guard, process pools and chunking, and sharing data between processes without paying too much for copying.

lessons.title: multiprocessing and start methods
objectives: Explain why processes give pure Python parallelism on the default build
Compare the spawn, fork and forkserver start methods
Write process-starting code that works on every operating system
key_points: multiprocessing runs functions in separate Python processes, each with its own interpreter and its own GIL, so CPU-bound Python code can use several cores at once. On the default build it's the standard way to run Python code in parallel.

The start method decides how a child process begins: spawn starts a fresh interpreter that imports your main module; fork copies the parent process as it is; forkserver forks each child from a small, clean server process started early on.

Defaults differ: spawn on Windows and macOS; fork on Linux up to Python 3.13 and forkserver from 3.14. fork is unsafe when the parent has other threads, as a child can inherit a lock some thread was holding, which is why the defaults moved away from it.

spawn and forkserver import the main module in every child, so the code that starts processes must sit under if __name__ == "__main__":. Without it, each child tries to start processes of its own and fails with a RuntimeError about the bootstrapping phase.

Arguments and results travel between processes by pickling, so worker functions must be defined at the top level of a module, not as lambdas or nested functions, and their data must be picklable. multiprocessing.get_context("spawn") picks a start method explicitly.

walkthrough.title: Start methods and the main-module guard

steps.do: Save start_method.py and run it with python start_method.py.
steps.code:
import multiprocessing as mp

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("default start method:", mp.get_start_method())
    print("available:", mp.get_all_start_methods())
steps.see: On Linux with Python 3.13: default start method: fork and available: ['fork', 'spawn', 'forkserver']. On macOS and Windows the default is spawn.

steps.do: Save no_guard.py, which starts a process with spawn but without the main-module guard, and run it with python no_guard.py.
steps.code:
import multiprocessing as mp


def work(x):
    print(x * 2)


ctx = mp.get_context("spawn")    # the default on Windows and macOS
p = ctx.Process(target=work, args=(21,))   # not protected by if __name__ == "__main__":
p.start()
p.join()
steps.see: A RuntimeError that begins An attempt has been made to start a new process before the current process has finished its bootstrapping phase, raised in the child, which imported the script and tried to start a process of its own.

steps.do: Fix it: put the three lines that create, start and join the process under the guard, and run it again.
steps.code:
if __name__ == "__main__":
    p = ctx.Process(target=work, args=(21,))
    p.start()
    p.join()

steps.do: Now try to send a lambda to a spawned process: change target=work to target=lambda x: print(x).
steps.see: _pickle.PicklingError: Can't pickle <function <lambda> ...>: attribute lookup <lambda> on __main__ failed. A function sent to another process must be importable by name.

lessons.title: Process pools: ProcessPoolExecutor and Pool
objectives: Run CPU-bound work in a ProcessPoolExecutor
Batch small tasks with chunksize to cut communication costs
Handle errors from workers and broken pools
key_points: ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=n) has the same submit, map and Future interface as the thread pool. Its default number of workers is the number of CPUs, a sensible ceiling for CPU-bound work.

Every task's arguments and result are pickled and sent through a pipe, so tiny tasks spend more time travelling than working. Batch them: pool.map(fn, items, chunksize=1000) sends items in groups, or make each task a whole range of the work.

An exception raised in a worker is pickled and re-raised in the parent when you call result() or reach it in map(). If a worker process dies outright, for example killed by the operating system for using too much memory, the pool breaks and raises BrokenProcessPool.
initializer=fn and initargs=(...) run once in each worker process as it starts: the place to load a large lookup table or a model once per process, rather than once per task.

multiprocessing.Pool is the older API (map, imap_unordered, starmap, apply_async) and is still common. ProcessPoolExecutor's futures make errors easier to handle and plug straight into asyncio through loop.run_in_executor.

lessons.title: Sharing data between processes
objectives: Explain why processes don't share Python objects
Pass data with Queue and Pipe, and share it with Value, Array and shared_memory
Keep the cost of copying data under control
key_points: Processes don't share Python objects: a global variable changed in a child changes only the child's copy. Results come back as return values, through a pool's futures, or as messages.
multiprocessing.Queue and Pipe send picklable objects between processes: a Queue can have many producers and consumers, while a Pipe connects exactly two ends.

multiprocessing.Value and Array keep simple C-typed data in shared memory, with a lock you take with get_lock(). multiprocessing.shared_memory.SharedMemory shares a raw block of bytes, such as the buffer behind a NumPy array, with no copying.

A Manager runs a server process that holds shared lists and dictionaries and gives other processes proxies to them. It's flexible, but every operation is a round trip to the manager, so it's slow for heavy use.

Copying is the hidden cost of multiprocessing: sending a large object with every task can cost more than the work itself. Send it once per worker with an initializer, put it in shared memory, or have each worker read its own slice from disk.

walkthrough.title: Shared memory, and a global that isn't shared

steps.code:
from multiprocessing import Process, Value

total = 0


def add(shared, n):
    global total
    total += n                       # changes this process's own copy only
    for _ in range(n):
        with shared.get_lock():      # a Value comes with its own lock
            shared.value += 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    shared = Value("i", 0)           # a C int in shared memory
    workers = [Process(target=add, args=(shared, 1000)) for _ in range(4)]
    for p in workers:
        p.start()
    for p in workers:
        p.join()
    print(f"shared counter: {shared.value}")
    print(f"global total in the parent: {total}")

lab.title: Use every core for a CPU-bound search
lab.goal: Split a CPU-bound search across a process pool, check that it finds the same answer as the sequential search, and measure how the number of chunks changes the time.
setup: Python 3.11 or later, on a computer with two or more CPU cores
Nothing else heavy running while you measure

steps.do: Read collatz.py. chain_length counts the steps a number takes to reach 1 in the Collatz sequence; longest_in_range finds the longest chain in a range; split cuts [1, LIMIT) into neighbouring ranges.
Check split before relying on it.
Write parallel_longest: map longest_in_range over split(limit, chunks) in a ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=workers), and return the max() of the results.
Run the script. It times the sequential search, then the parallel one with as many chunks as workers, and with eight times as many.

files.content:
"""Find the number below LIMIT with the longest Collatz chain: sequentially, then on every core."""
import os
import time
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

LIMIT = 300_000


def chain_length(n):
    steps = 0
    while n != 1:
        n = n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 * n + 1
        steps += 1
    return steps


def longest_in_range(bounds):
    """Return (steps, start) for the longest chain starting in [start, stop)."""
    start, stop = bounds
    return max((chain_length(n), n) for n in range(start, stop))


def split(limit, chunks):
    """Split [1, limit) into `chunks` neighbouring ranges."""
    edges = [1 + (limit - 1) * i // chunks for i in range(chunks + 1)]
    return list(zip(edges, edges[1:]))


def parallel_longest(limit, workers, chunks):
    # TODO: run longest_in_range over split(limit, chunks) in a ProcessPoolExecutor
    #       with `workers` processes, and return the best (steps, start) pair overall.
    raise NotImplementedError


def main():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    best = longest_in_range((1, LIMIT))
    print(f"sequential: longest chain below {LIMIT} starts at {best[1]} ({best[0]} steps)"
          f"  {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s")
    workers = os.cpu_count() or 1
    for chunks in (workers, workers * 8):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        result = parallel_longest(LIMIT, workers, chunks)
        print(f"parallel, {workers} workers, {chunks} chunks: starts at {result[1]} ({result[0]} steps)"
              f"  {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f}s  matches sequential: {result == best}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: pool.map(longest_in_range, split(limit, chunks)) gives one (steps, start) pair per chunk; max() of the pairs is the overall best, because tuples compare by their first item first.
Collatz chains vary a lot in length, so equal-sized ranges aren't equal amounts of work: with one chunk per worker, some workers finish early and sit idle.
If the parallel runs aren't faster, check os.cpu_count() and whether other programs are busy; on a single core, processes only add overhead.

modules.title: asyncio: the event loop, tasks and cancellation
modules.summary: Write concurrent code in a single thread with asyncio: coroutines and the event loop, tasks with gather and TaskGroup, timeouts and cancellation done safely, and the async building blocks: context managers, iterators, queues and semaphores.

lessons.title: Coroutines and the event loop
objectives: Explain how the event loop runs coroutines
Recognise and fix code that blocks the loop
Use asyncio's debug mode to find slow steps
key_points: async def defines a coroutine function. Calling it creates a coroutine object but runs none of its code until it's awaited or wrapped in a task; a coroutine that is never awaited triggers RuntimeWarning: coroutine ... was never awaited.

The event loop runs in one thread and switches between coroutines only at await points: a coroutine runs until it awaits something that isn't ready, and then the loop runs another. This is cooperative multitasking.
asyncio.run(main()) creates an event loop, runs main() to completion, cancels any tasks still running and closes the loop. Call it once, at the program's entry point.

A blocking call in a coroutine, such as time.sleep(), requests.get() or a long CPU loop, freezes every other coroutine. Use await asyncio.sleep() and async libraries, or move a blocking call to a thread with await asyncio.to_thread(fn, *args).

Debug mode, asyncio.run(main(), debug=True) or the environment variable PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1, logs every callback or task step that holds the loop for more than 100 milliseconds, and shows where never-awaited coroutines were created.

walkthrough.title: Block the event loop, then find it with debug mode

steps.do: Save blocking_loop.py. Three coroutines each wait 0.3 seconds, first with asyncio.sleep and then with time.sleep.
steps.code:
import asyncio
import time


async def tick(name, blocking):
    if blocking:
        time.sleep(0.3)              # blocks the whole event loop
    else:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.3)     # lets other coroutines run meanwhile
    return name


async def main(blocking):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    await asyncio.gather(*(tick(n, blocking) for n in "abc"))
    print(f"blocking={blocking}: {time.perf_counter() - start:.1f}s")


asyncio.run(main(blocking=False))
asyncio.run(main(blocking=True), debug=True)

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: blocking=False: 0.3s, then three debug-mode warnings like Executing <Task finished ... coro=<tick() done ...> took 0.300 seconds, then blocking=True: 0.9s.

steps.do: Fix the blocking branch by running the call in a thread, and run it again.
steps.see: Both runs take 0.3s and the warnings are gone.

steps.do: Add tick("z", False) on a line of its own at the start of main, without await, and run it.
steps.see: RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'tick' was never awaited. The call created a coroutine object and nothing ever ran it.

lessons.title: Tasks, gather and TaskGroup
objectives: Run coroutines concurrently with create_task and gather
Use TaskGroup for structured concurrency and handle ExceptionGroup with except*
Process results in the order they arrive
key_points: asyncio.create_task(coro()) schedules a coroutine to run concurrently and returns a Task. The event loop keeps only a weak reference to tasks, so keep your own (in a variable or a set) or a running task can be garbage-collected.

await asyncio.gather(a(), b()) runs awaitables concurrently and returns their results in the order given. By default the first exception goes straight to the caller while the others keep running; return_exceptions=True returns exceptions as results instead.

asyncio.TaskGroup (Python 3.11+), as in async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg: tg.create_task(...), waits for all its tasks when the block ends. If one fails, it cancels the rest and raises an ExceptionGroup, which except* handles by exception type.

Structured concurrency, which TaskGroup gives you, means no task outlives the block that started it, so failures aren't silently lost and clean-up is predictable. Prefer it to loose create_task calls in new code.

asyncio.as_completed(aws) yields awaitables in the order they finish, for handling results as they arrive; asyncio.wait(tasks, return_when=asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED) returns sets of done and pending tasks for finer control.

walkthrough.title: gather and TaskGroup side by side

steps.do: Save taskgroup.py.
steps.code:
import asyncio


async def fetch(name, seconds, fail=False):
    try:
        await asyncio.sleep(seconds)
        if fail:
            raise ValueError(f"{name} failed")
        print(f"{name} finished")
        return name
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print(f"{name} cancelled")
        raise                        # always let cancellation continue


async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(fetch("a", 0.1), fetch("b", 0.2))
    print("gather:", results)

    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            tg.create_task(fetch("c", 0.1, fail=True))
            tg.create_task(fetch("d", 1.0))
    except* ValueError as group:
        print("TaskGroup raised:", [str(e) for e in group.exceptions])


asyncio.run(main())

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: a finished, b finished, gather: ['a', 'b'], then d cancelled and TaskGroup raised: ['c failed']: when c failed, the group cancelled d.

steps.do: Make b fail too: change fetch("b", 0.2) to fetch("b", 0.2, fail=True) and run it again.
steps.see: a finished, then a traceback ending ValueError: b failed: gather passed the first exception straight to its caller, and the TaskGroup part never ran.

steps.do: Add return_exceptions=True to that gather call and run it.
steps.see: gather: ['a', ValueError('b failed')]: the exception comes back as a result, and the TaskGroup part runs as before.

lessons.title: Timeouts and cancellation
objectives: Bound how long an operation may take with asyncio.timeout and wait_for
Cancel tasks and clean up safely
Protect work that must finish with shield
key_points: task.cancel() asks a task to stop: CancelledError is raised inside it at the await where it's waiting. The coroutine can clean up in a finally block, or catch CancelledError to clean up, but must then re-raise it; swallowing it breaks timeouts and TaskGroup.

async with asyncio.timeout(2): (Python 3.11+) cancels the code inside if it runs longer than 2 seconds and turns the cancellation into TimeoutError as the block exits; await asyncio.wait_for(aw, timeout=2) does the same for a single awaitable.

From Python 3.11, asyncio.TimeoutError is the built-in TimeoutError, so catch TimeoutError. Put a timeout around a whole operation the caller cares about, such as a request with its retries, rather than around every step.
await asyncio.shield(aw) keeps the inner awaitable running when the outer await is cancelled: use it for work that must finish, such as saving a record. The outer await still raises CancelledError.

CancelledError is a subclass of BaseException, not Exception (since Python 3.8), so except Exception: doesn't swallow it. When asyncio.run finishes, or Ctrl+C cancels the main task, the remaining tasks are cancelled and their finally blocks run.

steps.do: Save timeouts.py.
steps.code:
import asyncio


async def slow_report():
    try:
        await asyncio.sleep(10)
        return "report"
    finally:
        print("slow_report: cleaning up")


async def main():
    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(0.2):
            await slow_report()
    except TimeoutError:
        print("timed out after 0.2s")

    task = asyncio.create_task(slow_report())
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    task.cancel()
    try:
        await task
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print("task cancelled:", task.cancelled())


asyncio.run(main())

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: slow_report: cleaning up, timed out after 0.2s, then slow_report: cleaning up and task cancelled: True: the finally block ran both times.

steps.do: Break the rule on purpose: add an except clause to slow_report that swallows the cancellation, just before finally:, and run it.
steps.see: Only the two cleaning up lines: the timeout no longer raises TimeoutError and the cancelled task returns normally, so the caller can't tell that either happened.

steps.do: Remove the except clause, so cancellation works again.

lessons.title: Async context managers, iterators, queues and semaphores
objectives: Write async context managers and async generators
Connect producers and consumers with asyncio.Queue
Limit concurrency with asyncio.Semaphore
key_points: async with calls __aenter__ and __aexit__, which can await, for resources whose set-up or tear-down does I/O, such as a connection pool or a transaction. contextlib.asynccontextmanager builds one from an async generator with a single yield.
async for loops over an asynchronous iterator, whose __anext__ can await. An async def function that contains yield is an async generator: a natural way to stream pages or messages as they arrive.

asyncio.Queue connects producer and consumer coroutines: await queue.put() waits while a bounded queue is full, await queue.get() waits for an item, and await queue.join() waits until task_done() has been called for every item.
asyncio.Semaphore(n) bounds concurrency: async with sem: lets at most n coroutines into a section at once, the usual way to limit how many requests go to a server at the same time.

asyncio's Lock, Event, Condition and Semaphore are for coroutines in one event loop and aren't thread-safe. To hand work to a loop from another thread, use asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro, loop) or loop.call_soon_threadsafe(callback).

steps.do: Save stream_queue.py: an async generator produces pages, five workers take them from a queue, a semaphore lets only three process at once, and an async context manager wraps the whole run.
steps.code:
import asyncio
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager


@asynccontextmanager
async def connection(name):
    print(f"open {name}")
    try:
        yield name
    finally:
        print(f"close {name}")


async def pages(n):                  # an async generator
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        await asyncio.sleep(0.01)    # waiting for the next page to arrive
        yield f"page-{i}"


async def worker(queue, sem, stats):
    while True:
        page = await queue.get()
        async with sem:              # at most 3 pages processed at once
            stats["now"] += 1
            stats["peak"] = max(stats["peak"], stats["now"])
            await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
            stats["now"] -= 1
        queue.task_done()


async def main():
    queue = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=4)
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(3)
    stats = {"now": 0, "peak": 0}
    async with connection("feed"):
        workers = [asyncio.create_task(worker(queue, sem, stats)) for _ in range(5)]
        async for page in pages(12):
            await queue.put(page)
        await queue.join()
        for w in workers:
            w.cancel()
    print(f"processed 12 pages, peak concurrency {stats['peak']}")


asyncio.run(main())

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: open feed, close feed, then processed 12 pages, peak concurrency 3.

steps.do: Change Semaphore(3) to Semaphore(10) and run it again.
steps.see: peak concurrency 5: now the five workers are the limit, not the semaphore.

steps.do: Make the queue unbounded (asyncio.Queue()), print queue.qsize() after each put, and run it. With maxsize=4 the producer waits whenever the workers fall behind; without it, the backlog can grow without limit.

lab.goal: Run a batch of jobs concurrently with asyncio, at most three at a time and each within a time limit, report every outcome, and test the runner with pytest.
setup: Python 3.11 or later (asyncio.timeout and TaskGroup arrived in 3.11)
pytest in your virtual environment: pip install pytest
The starter files jobs.py and test_jobs.py in one folder

Write run_job: inside async with sem:, call tracker.start(), then run work(...) inside async with asyncio.timeout(TIMEOUT): and return (name, "ok"). Catch TimeoutError for "timed out" and any other Exception for f"failed: {exc!r}", and call tracker.stop() in a finally block.

files.content:
"""Run a batch of jobs concurrently with asyncio: at most LIMIT at a time, each with a time limit."""
import asyncio

# (name, seconds the job takes, the error it raises or None)
JOBS = [
    ("alpha", 0.10, None),
    ("bravo", 5.00, None),          # far too slow: must time out
    ("charlie", 0.20, ValueError("bad input")),
    ("delta", 0.05, None),
    ("echo", 0.15, None),
    ("foxtrot", 5.00, None),        # too slow as well
    ("golf", 0.10, None),
    ("hotel", 0.05, None),
]
LIMIT = 3          # jobs running at once
TIMEOUT = 0.5      # seconds allowed for each job


class Tracker:
    """Counts the jobs running at once, and remembers the peak."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.running = 0
        self.peak = 0

    def start(self):
        self.running += 1
        self.peak = max(self.peak, self.running)

    def stop(self):
        self.running -= 1


async def work(name, seconds, error):
    await asyncio.sleep(seconds)
    if error:
        raise error
    return f"{name} done"


async def run_job(job, sem, tracker):
    """Run one job inside the semaphore and its timeout; return (name, status)."""
    name, seconds, error = job
    # TODO: 1. wait for a free place with `async with sem:`
    #       2. call tracker.start() as the job starts, and tracker.stop() in a finally block
    #       3. run work(name, seconds, error) inside `async with asyncio.timeout(TIMEOUT):`
    #       4. return (name, "ok"), (name, "timed out") or (name, f"failed: {exc!r}")
    raise NotImplementedError


async def main():
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(LIMIT)
    tracker = Tracker()
    # TODO: run run_job(job, sem, tracker) for every job in JOBS concurrently, with
    #       asyncio.TaskGroup (or asyncio.gather), and put the (name, status) pairs in results.
    results = []
    for name, status in sorted(results):
        print(f"{name:8} {status}")
    kinds = [status.split(":")[0] for _, status in results]
    print(f"summary: {kinds.count('ok')} ok, {kinds.count('timed out')} timed out, {kinds.count('failed')} failed")
    print(f"peak concurrency: {tracker.peak}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

hints: Put except TimeoutError before except Exception: except clauses are tried in order, and TimeoutError is an Exception too.
Don't catch BaseException or asyncio.CancelledError in run_job: a TaskGroup relies on cancellation reaching its tasks.
If peak concurrency shows 8, tracker.start() is outside async with sem:, or a new semaphore is being made for every job.

modules.title: Async HTTP, correctness and choosing a model
modules.summary: Call HTTP APIs concurrently with httpx, find and prevent race conditions and deadlocks in each model, and choose between threads, processes and asyncio from what a workload needs.

lessons.title: Async HTTP with httpx
objectives: Make concurrent HTTP requests with httpx.AsyncClient
Set timeouts and connection limits, and handle HTTP errors
Retry safely with backoff, and test without a network
key_points: httpx.AsyncClient is an async HTTP client with an API close to requests. Create one per application or job, as async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:, and reuse it: it keeps a pool of connections that later requests to the same host reuse.

httpx raises a timeout after 5 seconds of network inactivity by default; set your own with timeout=httpx.Timeout(10.0, connect=2.0). Timeouts raise httpx.TimeoutException and a refused connection raises httpx.ConnectError, both kinds of httpx.RequestError.
response.raise_for_status() raises httpx.HTTPStatusError for 4xx and 5xx responses. httpx.HTTPError is the base class of both HTTPStatusError and RequestError, for code that handles any failure.

httpx.Limits(max_connections=..., max_keepalive_connections=...) caps the client's pool, which allows 100 connections by default. An asyncio.Semaphore caps how many requests your code has in flight, set from what the server allows.

Retry only what may succeed next time and is safe to repeat, such as timeouts, 429 Too Many Requests and 503 Service Unavailable on GET requests. Wait longer each time (exponential backoff), add random jitter, and honour a Retry-After header.
httpx.MockTransport(handler) answers requests with a function you write instead of going to the network, so client code can be tested quickly and deterministically, failures included.

steps.do: Install httpx in your virtual environment.
Save httpx_basics.py. It fetches four items, two at a time, from a fake server built with MockTransport, so it needs no network.
steps.code:
import asyncio

import httpx


async def handler(request):
    """Stands in for a real server: replies after a short wait."""
    await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
    item = int(request.url.path.rsplit("/", 1)[-1])
    if item == 3:
        return httpx.Response(503, json={"error": "busy"})
    return httpx.Response(200, json={"id": item, "price": item * 1.5})


async def get_item(client, sem, item):
    async with sem:
        response = await client.get(f"/items/{item}")
    try:
        response.raise_for_status()
    except httpx.HTTPStatusError as exc:
        return f"item {item}: HTTP {exc.response.status_code}"
    return f"item {item}: {response.json()['price']}"


async def main():
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(2)
    transport = httpx.MockTransport(handler)          # leave this out to call a real server
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url="https://api.example.test", transport=transport,
                                 timeout=httpx.Timeout(2.0, connect=1.0)) as client:
        lines = await asyncio.gather(*(get_item(client, sem, i) for i in range(1, 5)))
    print("\n".join(lines))


asyncio.run(main())

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: item 1: 1.5, item 2: 3.0, item 3: HTTP 503, item 4: 6.0, in the order of the calls, because gather keeps order.

lessons.title: Race conditions and deadlocks
objectives: Recognise lost updates and check-then-act races in threads and in asyncio
Explain how deadlocks arise and prevent them
Diagnose a hang, and test concurrent code deterministically
key_points: A race condition is a bug whose outcome depends on timing. The common forms are the lost update, where two read-modify-write sequences overlap, and check-then-act, where state changes between checking it and acting on it, so two tasks both see the last seat free.

asyncio removes pre-emption but not races: any await between reading shared state and writing it lets another task run. Keep the check and the update together with no await in between, or hold an asyncio.Lock across both.

A deadlock is a cycle of waiting: thread 1 holds lock A and waits for lock B while thread 2 holds B and waits for A. Taking locks in one agreed order everywhere breaks the cycle, and so does never holding one lock while taking another.

Other common deadlocks: acquiring a non-reentrant lock (threading.Lock or asyncio.Lock) you already hold, a pool task waiting for another task queued behind it in the same full pool, and q.join() on a queue whose consumers have died.

Turn silent hangs into errors with timeouts: lock.acquire(timeout=5), future.result(timeout=5), asyncio.timeout(). To see where a hung program is stuck, use faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(seconds) or py-spy dump --pid PID, which print every thread's stack.

Test concurrent code by forcing the dangerous interleaving instead of hoping for it: use an Event or a Barrier, or await asyncio.sleep(0), to put tasks in the order that triggers the bug, then assert the fix holds. Never rely on sleeping for ordering.

walkthrough.title: A race in asyncio, and a deadlock you can see

steps.do: Save async_race.py. Two tasks each withdraw 80 from a balance of 100.
steps.code:
import asyncio


class Account:
    def __init__(self, balance):
        self.balance = balance
        self.lock = asyncio.Lock()

    async def withdraw_unsafe(self, amount):
        if self.balance >= amount:       # check
            await asyncio.sleep(0)       # any await lets another task run here
            self.balance -= amount       # act
            return True
        return False

    async def withdraw_safe(self, amount):
        async with self.lock:
            if self.balance >= amount:
                await asyncio.sleep(0)
                self.balance -= amount
                return True
            return False


async def main():
    for method in ("withdraw_unsafe", "withdraw_safe"):
        account = Account(100)
        results = await asyncio.gather(*(getattr(account, method)(80) for _ in range(2)))
        print(f"{method}: approved {results}, balance {account.balance}")


asyncio.run(main())

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: withdraw_unsafe: approved [True, True], balance -60, then withdraw_safe: approved [True, False], balance 20. In asyncio this interleaving is deterministic: both tasks pass the check before either one resumes.

steps.do: Save lock_order.py: two threads take the same two locks in opposite orders, and a Barrier makes sure each holds its first lock before it tries for the second.
steps.code:
import threading

lock_a, lock_b = threading.Lock(), threading.Lock()
both_holding = threading.Barrier(2)


def worker(name, first, second, patience):
    with first:
        both_holding.wait()                  # each thread now holds its first lock
        if second.acquire(timeout=patience): # a timeout turns a silent hang into an error
            second.release()
            print(f"{name}: got both locks")
        else:
            print(f"{name}: gave up waiting for its second lock")


t1 = threading.Thread(target=worker, args=("thread 1", lock_a, lock_b, 0.2))
t2 = threading.Thread(target=worker, args=("thread 2", lock_b, lock_a, 2.0))
t1.start(); t2.start()
t1.join(); t2.join()

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: thread 1: gave up waiting for its second lock, then thread 2: got both locks. Without the timeout, both threads would wait for ever.

steps.do: Make a hang visible: add import faulthandler and faulthandler.dump_traceback_later(1) at the top, change thread 1's patience from 0.2 to 10, and run it.
steps.see: Timeout (0:00:01)! and the stack of every thread, both workers stuck at the acquire line, before thread 2 gives up after two seconds.

steps.do: Now remove the deadlock at its cause: give thread 2 the locks in the same order as thread 1 (args=("thread 2", lock_a, lock_b, 2.0)), delete the both_holding.wait() line, and run it.
steps.see: thread 1: got both locks and thread 2: got both locks.

lessons.title: Choosing and combining models
objectives: Choose threads, processes or asyncio from a workload's needs
Combine asyncio with threads and processes
Set limits and measure before scaling up
key_points: Many waits with libraries that support async, such as HTTP clients, database drivers and websockets: asyncio, which keeps thousands of connections in progress in one thread, with little memory per task.

Blocking libraries, or a modest number of I/O jobs: a ThreadPoolExecutor, which needs no changes to existing synchronous code. CPU-bound pure Python: processes, sized to the number of cores, with work batched so that pickling stays small.

Inside asyncio, hand blocking calls to a thread with await asyncio.to_thread(fn, ...) and CPU-heavy work to a process pool with await loop.run_in_executor(pool, fn, ...), so the event loop keeps serving its other tasks.
NumPy, hashlib, zlib and many other C extensions release the GIL during long operations, so threads can run them in parallel even on the default build. Measure before reaching for processes.

On the free-threaded build, threads can run CPU-bound Python on several cores, but the build is newer, extension support varies and code that relied on the GIL may break. Check sys._is_gil_enabled() and test carefully before depending on it.

Start simple: write correct sequential code, measure where the time goes, add the simplest concurrency that removes the bottleneck, and set limits (workers, semaphores, timeouts) from what the systems downstream can take.

walkthrough.title: asyncio with threads and processes together

steps.do: Save combine.py: the event loop hands a blocking call to a thread and a CPU-heavy function to a process pool, and runs a coroutine of its own in the meantime.
steps.code:
import asyncio
import time
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor


def blocking_read(name):
    time.sleep(0.2)                  # a blocking library call
    return f"{name} read"


def cpu_heavy(n):
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        total = (total + i * i) % 1_000_003
    return total


async def main():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
        results = await asyncio.gather(
            asyncio.to_thread(blocking_read, "config"),             # blocking I/O: a thread
            loop.run_in_executor(pool, cpu_heavy, 2_000_000),       # CPU work: a process
            asyncio.sleep(0.1, result="the loop stayed free"),
        )
    print(results)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

steps.do: Run it.
steps.see: ['config read', 999912, 'the loop stayed free']

steps.do: Call the CPU-heavy function on the event loop instead: replace the run_in_executor line with the one below, and run the script in debug mode.
Run it with debug mode on (on Windows, pass debug=True to asyncio.run instead).
steps.see: A warning that Executing <Task pending name='Task-1' coro=<main() ...> took well over 0.100 seconds: the CPU-heavy call held the loop, then the same results.

files.content:
"""Fetch item prices from the local slow API: concurrently, politely and robustly."""
import asyncio
import random

import httpx

BASE_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8765"
MAX_IN_FLIGHT = 5            # requests in flight at once
ATTEMPTS = 3                 # tries per item, the first included
RETRY_STATUSES = {429, 503}  # worth trying again


class Stats:
    def __init__(self):
        self.in_flight = 0
        self.peak = 0
        self.retries = 0


async def fetch_price(client, item_id, sem, stats):
    """Return the item's price, or None if it doesn't exist.
    Raise httpx.TimeoutException if every attempt timed out."""
    # TODO: try up to ATTEMPTS times. For each attempt:
    #   - inside `async with sem:`, count the request in stats.in_flight (and update
    #     stats.peak), GET f"/items/{item_id}", and take it off the count in a finally block
    #   - 404: return None
    #   - a status in RETRY_STATUSES, or httpx.TimeoutException: unless this is the last
    #     attempt, add 1 to stats.retries and sleep 0.1 * 2 ** attempt seconds plus a little
    #     random jitter (random.uniform(0, 0.05)), then try again; on the last attempt,
    #     re-raise the timeout, or call response.raise_for_status()
    #   - otherwise call response.raise_for_status() and return response.json()["price"]
    raise NotImplementedError


async def fetch_all(ids, client):
    """Fetch every id concurrently; return ({id: price, None or "timed out"}, stats)."""
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(MAX_IN_FLIGHT)
    stats = Stats()
    results = {}

    async def one(item_id):
        try:
            results[item_id] = await fetch_price(client, item_id, sem, stats)
        except httpx.TimeoutException:
            results[item_id] = "timed out"

    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        for item_id in ids:
            tg.create_task(one(item_id))
    return dict(sorted(results.items())), stats


async def main():
    ids = list(range(1, 21)) + [101]
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url=BASE_URL, timeout=httpx.Timeout(1.0)) as client:
        results, stats = await fetch_all(ids, client)
    values = list(results.values())
    prices = [v for v in values if isinstance(v, float)]
    print(f"ok {len(prices)}, not found {values.count(None)}, timed out {values.count('timed out')}")
    print(f"total price {sum(prices):.2f}")
    print(f"retries {stats.retries}, peak in flight {stats.peak}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

hints: Give each attempt its own async with sem: block, so a task waiting out its backoff doesn't hold a place that another request could use.
httpx.TimeoutException covers connect, read, write and pool timeouts. Catch it around the request, and re-raise it on the last attempt so that fetch_all records timed out.
If retries is 2 instead of 4, timeouts aren't being retried; if it's higher, you may be retrying 404s, or retrying after the last attempt.
pytest.raises(ExceptionGroup) catches what the TaskGroup raises; its .exceptions attribute holds the HTTPStatusError.
The server alternates 503s and successes for ids divisible by 7. If a run stopped half-way, restart slow_server.py so the next run starts in step.

project.title: Build a concurrent price aggregator
project.brief: A purchasing team needs a daily report on everything a supplier sells: each product's name, mean recent price and a risk score. The supplier's API, which you run locally with supplier_server.py, is slow and unreliable: product ids come in pages, some requests fail with 503 until retried, some always fail with 500, and a few take far too long. The risk score (risk_score in scoring.py) is pure Python and CPU-heavy. Build aggregate.py, a command-line tool that walks the listing pages, fetches every product concurrently with httpx.AsyncClient within a concurrency limit, retries what's worth retrying with backoff and jitter, gives up on slow requests with timeouts, scores products in a ProcessPoolExecutor through loop.run_in_executor so the event loop never blocks, and writes report.csv sorted by id. Ctrl+C must stop it cleanly: cancel outstanding work, close the client and the pool, and write a partial report clearly marked as incomplete. Against the provided server, a correct run scores 192 products and reports 4 that failed with HTTP 500 and 4 that timed out.
deliverables: aggregate.py, with command-line options for the base URL, the concurrency limit, the timeout and the number of worker processes
report.csv from a full run: id, name, mean_price, risk_score and status for all 200 products
pytest tests using httpx.MockTransport for paging, a retried 503, a 500 that isn't retried, a timeout and the concurrency limit
A test that forces the interleaving to prove one piece of shared state (such as your counters or results) is safe
DESIGN.md: which model does what and why, the limits you chose (concurrency, timeouts, retries, workers) and how you'd set them for a real supplier
Timings for at least three configurations, such as 1, 2 and 4 worker processes, with an explanation of what limits the throughput

rubric.name: Correct results
rubric.description: report.csv is complete and sorted by id, with the right statuses: 192 scored, 4 HTTP 500 and 4 timed out against the provided server, the same on every run.

rubric.name: Concurrency design
rubric.description: Network I/O runs on asyncio with a bounded number of requests in flight, scoring runs in a process pool through run_in_executor, and nothing blocks the event loop.

rubric.name: Robustness
rubric.description: Every request has a timeout; only timeouts, 429 and 503 are retried, with exponential backoff and jitter; 500s and 404s aren't retried; Ctrl+C shuts down cleanly and closes the client and the pool.

rubric.name: Tests
rubric.description: MockTransport tests cover paging, retries, failures, timeouts and the concurrency limit, plus a deterministic race test; all pass without a network and without sleeping for ordering.

rubric.name: Measurement and explanation
rubric.description: Timings for several configurations, and a clear explanation, in DESIGN.md, of what limits throughput and why the chosen limits suit the supplier.

rubric.name: Code quality
rubric.description: Readable, well-named functions with type hints and docstrings, and settings taken from command-line options rather than edited constants.

project.submit: Paste aggregate.py, your test file and its pytest summary line, the tool's summary output with the first ten lines of report.csv, your timings, and DESIGN.md.
